title: Americans value First Amendment freedoms while knowledge gaps, self-censorship and surveillance concerns constrain everyday participation
source_unit: Freedom Forum, The First Amendment: Where America Stands 2026
geography: United States; adults aged 16 and older, with selected college, generational, racial/ethnic, education and income comparisons

denominator.unit: online U.S. respondents aged 16 and older

first_amendment_vital.unit: percent saying the First Amendment is vital to America

campus_free_exchange.unit: percent saying college campuses should foster a free exchange of ideas

hate_speech_awareness.unit: percent correctly recognizing that the First Amendment protects hate speech

observations.method: Annual Freedom Forum online survey designed and conducted for the organization by McKee Wallwork and Decision Analyst using proprietary research methodologies; respondents were drawn from American Consumer Opinion, Decision Analyst and partner panels and could respond in English or Spanish.
observations.uncertainty: The sample is an online panel rather than a probability sample of all U.S. residents, and the publicly released report is an overview while full survey results are available upon request; subgroup margins may be higher than the overall ±3.4 percentage points.
observations.subgroup: U.S. respondents aged 16 and older, including college students, Gen Z and other generations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Valuing a constitutional freedom and believing it goes too far can coexist because respondents may support the principle while disagreeing about specific applications, tradeoffs or groups protected.

observations.period: 2026 survey; reported reasons for not speaking freely

denominator.unit: online U.S. respondents aged 16 and older

do_not_speak_freely.unit: percent saying they do not speak freely

fear_violent_response.unit: percent citing fear of a violent response

fear_family_tension.unit: percent citing fear of creating tension with friends or family

surveillance_discourages_protest.unit: percent saying surveillance technologies discouraged protest participation

observations.method: Self-reported online survey questions about speech, participation and perceived deterrents; multiple reasons could be selected.
observations.uncertainty: The survey measures perceived inhibition rather than observed speech, protest or political-group participation and cannot identify whether surveillance, violence, family tension or other factors caused withdrawal.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults and older teens, with college-student, generational and racial/ethnic comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: The report also finds that the share saying nothing keeps them from speaking freely has risen to 36% and that deterrence measures have declined since 2024, so the pattern is not uniformly worsening.

observations.period: 2026 survey; First Amendment knowledge and practical understanding

denominator.unit: online U.S. respondents aged 16 and older

say_informed.unit: percent saying they are informed about First Amendment rights

name_all_five.unit: percent able to name all five freedoms without prompting

name_none.unit: percent unable to name a single freedom without prompting

private_workplace_misconception.unit: percent incorrectly believing the First Amendment applies to private workplaces

education_gradient.value: 20% of advanced-degree respondents versus 8% of respondents with a high-school education or less could name all five freedoms

observations.method: Unaided knowledge questions and self-assessed knowledge in the Freedom Forum survey.
observations.uncertainty: Naming a freedom is only one measure of civic knowledge; the survey does not test legal reasoning, actual rights exercise, classroom instruction or whether greater knowledge changes behavior.
observations.subgroup: U.S. respondents aged 16 and older, with education and generation comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap between confidence and unaided recall may reflect the difference between abstract awareness and practical application rather than simple civic indifference.

observations.period: 2026 survey; online information, government control and press legitimacy

denominator.unit: online U.S. respondents aged 16 and older

government_transparency_social_media.unit: percent saying government should be transparent about communication with social media companies about content moderation

concern_government_control.unit: percent concerned government has too much control over what can be said in media or online

verify_online_images.unit: percent using some method to verify online images and videos

always_trust_online_media.unit: percent always trusting images and videos posted online from the media

news_watchdog.unit: percent saying it is important for news media to serve as a government watchdog

observations.method: Self-reported survey measures of digital trust, verification, content moderation and press roles.
observations.uncertainty: The findings describe public judgments and reported verification, not the accuracy of verification, the content people encounter, platform enforcement or the effects of government-platform communication.
observations.subgroup: U.S. respondents aged 16 and older, with Gen Z reporting higher verification than older generations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Skepticism toward online media and government control can support verification and oversight, but it can also make shared factual authority harder to sustain.

related_sources.claim: Official 2026 survey overview with findings, subgroup comparisons and link to the report.
Freedom Forum release describing the 2026 survey launch, headline findings and field dates.

boundary: This record captures a civic-legitimacy and participation signal: Americans broadly value First Amendment freedoms while practical knowledge, expression confidence, surveillance concerns, online verification and views of government-platform control shape how those freedoms are experienced. The source is an advocacy-organization-sponsored online panel survey with proprietary methods and an overview of publicly released results; it is not a probability-sample population estimate, legal assessment, behavioral trace, causal participation study or measure of actual government censorship.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Freedom Forum 2026 report and survey overview were browser-reviewed for field dates, sample size, margin of error, First Amendment valuation, speech inhibition, knowledge, surveillance, online verification, press and government-control findings. The public PDF endpoint was not directly retrievable from the shell, so the stored fingerprint is a SHA-256 of the canonical report URL rather than a downloaded-file hash.
